title: Your Eggs Could Have Salmonella. Here’s How to Make Them Safer
gist: Facing multi-state salmonella recalls that include eggs from Midwest Poultry Services sold under five brand names, WIRED tests home egg pasteurization with an Anova sous vide circulator at 135°F for 90 minutes. Experts confirm the method makes eggs safer for raw preparations but warn it may not kill all salmonella, and that the circulator's come-up time doesn't count toward the kill step.

insights.claim: Eggs remain the single food commodity most associated with outbreak illnesses, according to an infectious disease director, making them a structurally higher-risk category than the recall cycle alone suggests.
insights.so_what: Category-level risk ranking matters more than individual recalls for anyone assessing food-supply liability exposure.
insights.quote: “eggs remain the single food commodity most associated with outbreak illnesses,”
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: The USDA has estimated that 1 in every 20,000 eggs is contaminated with salmonella, which against 67 billion US eggs produced annually implies about 3 million potentially dangerous eggs per year.
insights.so_what: Quantifies the residual risk that regulation has failed to eliminate — a small per-unit probability across an enormous denominator.
insights.quote: at one point, the USDA estimated that 1 out of every 20,000 eggs was thought to be contaminated with salmonella
insights.locator: It's difficult to tell just by looking
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: The USDA enacted a 72-page egg safety requirement in 2009 intending to eradicate contamination, and contamination has clearly not been eradicated.
insights.so_what: A documented case of regulation failing to close a contamination pathway — relevant to how much comfort compliance frameworks should provide.
insights.quote: The USDA enacted a 72-page egg safety requirement in 2009 in hopes of eradicating contamination, but clearly, it hasn't happened.
insights.locator: The USDA enacted a 72-page egg safety requirement
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: Salmonella can reach an egg either externally via contact with droppings or internally, deposited inside the egg from an infected chicken's ovaries — so shell washing alone cannot guarantee safety.
insights.so_what: Internal contamination is the mechanism that defeats surface-level controls and forces thermal treatment as the only reliable kill step.
insights.quote: which can be transferred to the shell from contact with droppings or even deposited inside the egg itself from an infected chicken's ovaries
insights.locator: Chickens and other poultry commonly carry
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: The July 2026 egg recall traced to a single supplier, Midwest Poultry Services, but the eggs were sold under five brand names including Kroger and Simple Truth.
insights.so_what: Private-label consolidation means one supplier failure propagates across multiple retail brands — a hidden concentration risk in grocery.
insights.quote: Though the eggs being recalled are only from one supplier, Midwest Poultry Services, they were sold under five brand names
insights.locator: Though the eggs being recalled are only from one supplier
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: The vast majority of US shell eggs are not pasteurized because holding 130 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit without cooking the egg is tricky; pasteurized eggs are more expensive and labeled as such.
insights.so_what: A process-difficulty constraint, not a cost-of-goods one, keeps pasteurized eggs a niche premium product.
insights.quote: Because this is tricky, the vast majority of eggs sold in the US are not pasteurized
insights.locator: If you want to be certain a whole, raw shell egg
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: Liquid eggs sold in cartons are all pasteurized but contain only egg whites, not yolks, so they cannot substitute for whole raw eggs in recipes like mayonnaise, aioli, eggnog or royal icing.
insights.so_what: Defines the unserved product gap: a shelf-stable pasteurized whole-egg product for raw applications.
insights.quote: While in-shell eggs aren't pasteurized, all liquid eggs are—the kind in the carton. However, these are just egg whites, not yolks
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: An infectious disease director specifies that killing salmonella in eggs requires the egg center to be held near 135 degrees for close to one hour, and that the circulator's come-up time does not count toward that duration.
insights.so_what: The come-up-time exclusion is the failure mode most home procedures get wrong — timing starts at temperature, not at power-on.
insights.quote: The ‘come up’ time for the circulator to reach the appropriate temperature does not count and will not kill salmonella.”
insights.locator: Though Bulbin said he does not have direct experience
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: A microbiologist confirms the sous vide process makes eggs safer but cautions it may not kill all salmonella present, so immunocompromised or otherwise susceptible people should consider other cooking options.
insights.so_what: Risk reduction is not elimination — an honest caveat that separates this from a marketing claim.
insights.quote: sous vide may not kill all of the salmonella that might be present in the eggs, so people who are immunocompromised or otherwise more susceptible to salmonella infection might want to consider other cooking options to be truly safe.”
insights.locator: “We can say that sous vide process will make eggs safer
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: Eggs should be refrigerated before sous vide treatment because cold storage keeps any salmonella present from replicating, ensuring starting bacterial levels are low.
insights.so_what: Starting load determines whether a fixed time-temperature treatment is sufficient — the cold chain is part of the kill step, not separate from it.
insights.quote: “because this helps to keep any salmonella that may be present in the eggs from replicating, thus ensuring that starting levels of salmonella are low.”
insights.locator: She also notes that eggs should be stored
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: After 90 minutes at 135 degrees the tested eggs showed only minor cloudiness in the white and were usable as normal raw eggs, though denatured proteins mean no stellar foaming or stiff-peak performance.
insights.so_what: The functional cost of home pasteurization is meringue performance, which bounds which recipes it actually serves.
insights.quote: pasteurizing eggs denatures the proteins, and so will affect egg whites’ performance—don't expect to be making any pasteurized-egg soufflés or pavlovas
insights.locator: Part of the challenge with pasteurization
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: Circulators can vary by at least 1 degree, so the microbiologist recommends verifying with a probe thermometer and possibly adjusting time for small versus large eggs.
insights.so_what: Device calibration error is inside the safety margin at 135 degrees — an independent measurement is required, not optional.
insights.quote: circulators can vary by at least 1 degree, so it's a good idea to double-check with a probe thermometer
insights.locator: I attached the Anova to a clean pot
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: Sous vide immersion circulators originated in laboratory settings for incubating cultures and sterilizing equipment before chefs adopted them in the 1970s and '80s, which is why they are well suited to precise pasteurization.
insights.so_what: The lab lineage explains the temperature precision that makes the food-safety application credible rather than improvised.
insights.quote: Sous vide immersion circulators actually originated in laboratory settings as a way to incubate cultures and sterilize testing equipment
insights.locator: Sous vide immersion circulators actually originated
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: Anova has been building water baths for industrial and scientific customers since 2003 and circulators since 2007, and WIRED rated this model's predecessor 9/10 in 2013.
insights.so_what: A two-decade instrument pedigree is the credibility basis for a consumer kitchen brand entering a safety-critical use case.
insights.quote: building water baths for the industrial and scientific community since 2003, and circulators since 2007
insights.locator: I attempted to pasteurize some eggs I bought at Costco
insights.speaker: Kat Merck

insights.claim: Eggs should be kept refrigerated at 42 degrees Fahrenheit or less as standard practice, and fully cooking eggs to a firm yolk and white removes salmonella as a concern without any pasteurization step.
insights.so_what: The 90-minute procedure is only relevant to raw and near-raw preparations; ordinary cooking already solves the problem.
insights.quote: As long as your eggs are “cooked thoroughly, with a firm yolk and white,” according to Bulbin, salmonella shouldn't be a concern.
insights.locator: It's good practice to always keep your eggs refrigerated
insights.speaker: Kat Merck
